newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica looks at "attractive" foreign arms offers.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica looks at "attractive" foreign arms offers.

text.p: South Africa is being courted by foreign countries offering attractive arms sales contracts, the head of the Armscor weapons buying agency said on Wednesday.
"They want to sell us product now, but we are saying we must use this policy whereby there will be off-sets and counter-trades," Armscor chairman Ron Haywood told a parliamentary defence committee.

"Some of the countries are coming to us with economic packages and saying, 'we're prepared to look at investment, job creation, empowerment, research, of the value of a rand for a rand', or more...That's not a bad deal," he said.
Parliament is expected to give final approval next week to a review of defence needs which would allow for the purchase of, among other things, four navy corvettes.
Britain, Spain, Germany and France are among countries known to be interested in supplying the ships.
"They are coming with packages that I think will be quite attractive," Haywood said. "That will happen in the next few months. It's a long process to evaluate them."
He said approval of the defence review would be welcomed by the domestic defence industry.

"There's been such uncertainty in the past. You live through almost every year not knowing what the budget's likely to end up being... Now we would like to believe there should be some stabilising of budgets," he said.
He said the review envisaged allocating about 30 percent of the defence budget on capital expenditure.

"We're down to about 15 percent on capital expenditure which is very much lower than it's ever been and perhaps just a little bit too low, especially when we have a lot of equipment that's ageing considerably," Haywood said.
He said if spending remained low, South Africa risked losing the capacity to make helicopters such as the Rooivalk and to stay abreast of electronic warfare and stealth technology.

"If we do not have enough research, we're back to 1945 -- the end of the last war where we were making a few vehicles and some explosives and lost some key technologies. That's the thing South Africa has to guard against," he said.
